output.title: Exception queues are the right place to start
output.body:
Before you automate anything, look at the exception queue first. That is the work that falls outside the main workflow: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or other cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot name the queue, you usually cannot automate it cleanly either.

The useful question is not “can this be automated?” It is: which exceptions arrive often enough to matter, and which ones are just one-offs? For one week, track three things for one queue: how many exceptions appear, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then sort the queue into routine, mixed, or ad-hoc.

Routine exceptions are the clearest candidates for a narrow automation pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad-hoc work often stays manual because there is no stable pattern for the software to follow.

Keep the control rules visible while you do this. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can organise the review, but it does not replace the person who owns the decision.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. A short, honest inventory of one exception queue is usually enough to show whether the next step is a tool change, a hiring decision, or a narrow pilot. Very unglamorous. Usually useful.
